aide.views.def.railJour: The same day as the day calendar, but seen per person: one line per animateur, vacations placed in time. Gaps, spans and back-to-back chains show at a glance, and empty lines say who is still callable — the ones marked “unavailable” say the opposite: do not call on that person. A vacation can be dragged onto another line: that person takes it, or swaps their own if they already work at that hour, under the same conditions as on the day calendar.
aide.views.def.repos: The other views turned around: not who is where, but who gets a breather. One line per staff member, one column per day of the event, and only three states — working day (with the number of hours), rest day, unavailable. A rest day is a day the person could have worked and the schedule did not assign them to; a day they declared unavailable is not one, they could not be called on. The most strained lines come first: those chaining the most consecutive working days, and those with no free day at all. The « Run » column gives that longest run, and the table footer says how many people rest each day — hence how many are left to call. A red cell flags an assignment placed on a day declared unavailable: an anomaly of the plan, to be fixed.
aide.views.def.graphe: The same data taken from the ground: a location, the stands standing on it, the time slots they are staffed on, who is assigned there. One column per level, click to open the next one. This is the view for whoever knows the site plan better than the list of stands. The last two columns read from the saved schedule and stay empty until a solve has run; the locations and their stands come from the reference data and can be browsed straight away.
aide.views.def.kpi: One line per completed solve, across all editions: score, coverage, spread of hours, number of manual changes, duration. It is the memory of past campaigns — it says whether the current edition is settling better or worse than the previous one, and how many manual fixes it took. Nothing in it is nominative, and the history outlives the deletion of the edition it describes.

You do it from the “My availability” tab, on your phone: the days of the event show as chips, tap the ones that do not work.

aide.dispo.title: Availability and preference collection
aide.dispo.summary: Animateurs declare their own unavailable days and wishes; you apply them, or not.
aide.dispo.intro: Before building a schedule you need to know who cannot come when. Rather than collecting that outside the application and typing it back in, you open a collection window: every animateur declares from their espace, on their phone, the days they are unavailable and the kinds of games they would like to run. What they send touches nothing: it is a proposal, waiting for your decision on the Availability screen.
aide.dispo.def.fenetre: The “Collection window” panel, at the top of the Availability page, carries the two buttons “Open collection” and “Close collection”. It is closed until you open it — unlike the swap fair, which is open by default. Both dates are optional: they bound the period, the switch stays in charge. Closed, the espace refuses any declaration server-side, not merely on screen; the animateur keeps access to what they declared and to your answers.
aide.dispo.def.prevenir: A checkbox at opening time, never a permanent setting: it sends everyone the link to their espace, straight to the declaration tab. Tick it on the first round; leave it alone when you reopen the window after a correction, or everybody gets a reminder for nothing. The report names those without an e-mail address and the failed sends.
aide.dispo.term.decision: Apply or refuse, as a whole
aide.dispo.def.decision: The screen shows side by side what the animateur declares and what their record says today. Applying writes the whole proposal onto their record, exactly as if you had opened it to edit it — the stored schedule is then flagged as stale, and regenerating stays a separate action from the Solver page. Refusing changes nothing; the reason you type is read by the animateur in their espace. There is deliberately no line-by-line approval: a disagreement is settled with a word, and the animateur sends a corrected version.
aide.dispo.def.remplacement: An animateur correcting themself replaces their pending proposal, they do not stack a second one: you will never have to arbitrate two contradictory versions of the same person, and what reaches you is always the latest. You are e-mailed when a proposal lands on your desk, not on every correction they make to it before you process it.
aide.dispo.def.competences: Skills stay decided with you. A self-declared skill feeds hard rules — who may staff which stand — and the stakes are not those of an unavailability or a wish, which can be caught up. An animateur declaring a day outside the dates of the event, or a game category that does not exist, is refused on submission.

aide.shortcuts.intro: Ctrl+K opens the command palette: a single field that leads to any page of the application and also searches the reference data — a staff member (their timeline opens), a stand or a time slot (the calendar opens on it). The arrow keys walk the list, Enter opens, Esc closes. This is the one to remember: every other shortcut is only a shorthand for something the palette already does.
aide.shortcuts.def.palette: Opens (and closes) the command palette. The browser does not receive this shortcut while a tab of the application is in the foreground.
aide.shortcuts.def.help: Shows the full list of shortcuts, without leaving the current screen.
aide.shortcuts.def.filter: Puts the caret in the filter of the current page, when it has one (the reference-data pages, and this help page).
aide.shortcuts.def.submit: Submits the form being filled in, like a click on its save button. A form whose button is disabled (an incomplete entry) is not saved for all that: the keyboard does nothing the mouse is refused.
aide.shortcuts.def.escape: Closes the open window (palette, form, confirmation) and gives the focus back to wherever it was opened from.
aide.shortcuts.go: To jump straight to a screen, type “g” then the letter of the destination — “g” then “a” for the staff members. Pages with no letter remain reachable through the palette, which lists them all.
aide.shortcuts.tables: The reference-data tables (staff, stands, time slots, locations, game categories) are keyboard-navigable too. The shortest way in: “/” puts the cursor in the page filter, type enough to narrow the list, then Arrow down jumps straight onto the first row. Tab enters them too, on a single row — never row by row — but it first walks through the header controls (the “select all” checkbox and every sortable header). The arrow keys then move the focus one step at a time; Tab leaves the row towards its buttons, then towards the rest of the page.
aide.shortcuts.def.rowEnter: Enters the table without counting tab stops: the focus jumps onto the current row, the one an outline marks. This is the gesture to remember — filter, then go down. Clicking a row focuses it the same way, and the arrow keys carry on from there.

aide.importGrille.title: Stand grid import
aide.importGrille.summary: Pour in the workbook matrix — stands as rows, days and slots as columns — without retyping it: expected format, what each column does, and what an imported stand becomes.
aide.importGrille.format: The “Stand grid import” screen reads a CSV as a spreadsheet exports it: a first column naming the stand by its id or its exact name, then one column per day and per créneau, a headcount per cell, blank, “-” or 0 for closed. Two header lines — the dates, a spreadsheet's merged cells leaving the following ones blank, then the bands “10h00-12h00” or “10:00-12:00” — or a single one, “2026-07-08 10h00-12h00”. The “Download the current grid as a template” button renders the edition as it stands, in that exact format: starting from it is the simplest way. The template writes its bands with an “h” on purpose: Excel turns “13:00-16:00” into the date-time “30/11/1999 13:16:00”, and the band is then lost.
aide.importGrille.colonnes: Each column lands on the créneau of the same date that contains its hours; a column narrower than its créneau writes a window at its own bounds, the rest of the créneau left as it was. A column no créneau contains — a set-up band the edition does not have, a comment column — is ignored and listed, without the file being refused. A créneau the file does not name keeps each imported stand's current cell, windows included: the import only rewrites what the file states. With no créneau at all in the edition, the import is refused: create them first, as a series or derived from the stands' hours.
aide.importGrille.stands: An accepted stand is rewritten as from the entry grid: its whole schedule follows its cells, folded into rules where a pattern repeats, and its minimum and maximum headcounts follow the smallest and largest cell. A stand absent from the file is untouched, and the import creates no stand: an unknown id, or a name two stands share, rejects the row and says so. Nothing is written before “Import”, and the write is all of a piece.

aide.competences.title: Skills grid
aide.competences.summary: Type every animateur's appreciation on every game category in one grid, from the keyboard, alongside their wishes — and exchange it as a CSV that never removes anything.
aide.competences.grille: The animateur record types appreciations one person at a time; the “Skills” screen shows them all at once, animateurs in rows and game categories in columns. A cell carries the level — empty, beginner, autonomous or referent — and changes with a click (the levels cycle) or a key: 0 empties the cell, 1, 2 and 3 set the level; the arrows, Enter, Home and End move the selection as in a spreadsheet, and arrow down from the filter enters the grid. Nothing is written before “Save”: changed cells are outlined and the button counts the records involved; “Discard changes” restores the grid as it was read, and leaving the page with unsaved cells asks for confirmation. A small heart in a cell says the animateur declared a wish for that game category: the appreciation is typed in sight of the wish, neither deciding the other. The ninja game category's column is marked — holding it makes an animateur versatile — and follows the usual rule. The name filter and the chosen columns stay in the page's address, hence in a shared link.
aide.competences.concurrence: Saving writes one record per modified row, each with its own concurrent-modification guard: if another session modified a record after the grid was opened, that row alone is refused, the others are written, and the screen asks — as for a record — to reload or to knowingly overwrite. Dismissing the question leaves the row as typed, unsent. While a solve runs, typing is locked: the solver would rewrite the records when it lands.
aide.competences.csv: “Export as CSV” renders the grid as it stands: an “animateur” column with the id — never the name —, then one column per game category named by its id, and in each cell DEBUTANT, AUTONOME, REFERENT or nothing. “Import a CSV” reads that same format, after a row-by-row preview like the other imports: nothing is written before “Import”, then everything in one go. A row names an animateur by id — unknown, it is rejected, the import creates no record; a column naming no game category is ignored and listed; an unreadable level rejects its row. The point that matters: an empty cell of the file leaves the appreciation as it is. The import adds and updates, it never removes — removing an appreciation stays a gesture of the grid on screen. A file exported then re-imported unchanged therefore writes nothing, and says so.
